description: The Toshiba EM925A5A leads 5 small microwaves; 0.7 cu ft models cook at about 700 watts and 0.9 cu ft at 900. Sized for RVs, dorms and power stations.
dek: The Toshiba EM925A5A leads 5 small microwaves; 0.7 cu ft models cook at about 700 watts and 0.9 cu ft at 900.
intro: Five compact microwaves worth buying for a small kitchen, a dorm room or an RV, and the input-watt math that decides whether one will run on your power station or generator.

A small microwave is the easiest appliance in the house to buy and the easiest to get wrong once it leaves the house. The number printed on the box is cooking power, not what it pulls from the wall, and that gap is the whole story when the outlet is a power station, an inverter or a camping generator.

sections.h: What Small Really Means in a Microwave

blocks.p: Microwaves are sold by interior capacity in cubic feet, and the compact end of the market runs from about 0.6 to 0.9 cubic feet. A 0.7 cubic foot model is the classic dorm and office size: it fits a standard dinner plate on a turntable in the 10-inch range, reheats a mug of coffee or a bowl of soup without fuss, and sits on a counter about the width of a large toaster oven. A 0.9 cubic foot model adds enough room for a taller casserole dish or a bag of popcorn that does not scrape the ceiling, and it usually comes with a jump from 700 to 900 cooking watts.

The capacity number is only half of the fit question. Exterior width, depth and the swing of the door decide whether the thing actually goes where you want it. Compact models are generally somewhere between 17 and 20 inches wide and 13 to 16 inches deep, but those numbers vary by a couple of inches between brands at the same capacity, and a couple of inches is everything in an RV galley or a dorm shelf. Measure the space, subtract the ventilation clearance the manual asks for, and only then shop. We cover clearances properly later in this guide.

Smaller also means lower power, and that is not purely a downside. A 700-watt machine takes longer to heat a frozen dinner than a 1,100-watt family model, often by a minute or two, and package instructions are usually written for 1,000 watts or more. But a 700-watt microwave is also the one most likely to run on a mid-size portable power station or a small inverter generator. For anyone who cooks off-grid, in a camper or during outages, that trade is the reason to buy small in the first place.

There is one category we deliberately left out: the so-called portable microwave for a car. Most products sold under that phrase are actually heated lunch boxes, which warm food slowly through a heating plate and are not microwaves at all. True 12-volt microwaves have existed as niche products, but we could not find one currently in wide distribution that we were confident recommending. If what you need is a hot lunch in a truck cab, our guide to the best heated lunch box is the honest answer. If you want a real microwave in a vehicle, you need a 120-volt model, an inverter and a battery bank sized for it.

Finally, small does not mean cheap in the bad sense. The compact class is crowded with no-name units that look identical, and the differences show up in door latches, control panels and turntable motors after a year of use. Every pick here comes from a brand with long-running retail distribution, which matters when a turntable coupler or a glass tray breaks and you want a replacement part rather than a new microwave.

sections.h: Cooking Watts vs Input Watts: The Number That Matters Off-Grid

blocks.p: Every microwave has two power figures, and only one of them is on the front of the box. The headline number, 700 watts or 900 watts or 1,200 watts, is cooking power: the microwave energy delivered into the cavity. The second number is input power, what the appliance pulls from the outlet to make that cooking power. It is printed on the rating label inside the door frame or on the back, and in the manual's specification table. For a typical household microwave, input is roughly 1.5 times the cooking rating.

That ratio comes from the losses inside the machine. A conventional microwave runs a high-voltage transformer feeding a magnetron, and both the transformer and the magnetron give off a lot of heat, which is why there is a cooling fan running the whole time. Add the turntable motor and the interior light, and a 700-watt microwave commonly draws around 1,000 to 1,100 watts from the wall, a 900-watt model somewhere around 1,350 to 1,450 watts, and a 1,200-watt model in the 1,500 to 1,600 watt range. Always check your specific model's label, because some run a little higher or lower than the rule of thumb.
THE RULE
Size your power source to input watts, not cooking watts.

A 1000W microwave in the sense people search for is usually a 1,000-watt cooking model that pulls roughly 1,500 watts from the outlet. Read the input figure on the rating label, then add headroom of at least 20 percent for the start-up surge and for an inverter that is running warm.

There is also a start-up surge. Conventional transformer-based microwaves draw a brief inrush when the magnetron circuit energizes, and that spike is higher than the steady running figure. A power station or inverter that can hold the running load can still trip on the first second of every cooking cycle if its surge rating is thin. This is the single most common reason people report that a microwave works on one power station and fails on another with the same continuous rating.

Power level settings do not change the peak draw on a conventional microwave. At 50 percent, a non-inverter model cycles the magnetron fully on and fully off, so it hits the same full input wattage for part of each cycle. The average energy use drops, which helps a battery last longer, but the inverter or generator still has to handle the full draw every time the magnetron kicks in. Inverter microwaves behave differently, which is the subject of a later section.

Energy use, as opposed to power, is easier on a battery than people expect. A 700-watt microwave pulling about 1,050 watts for three minutes uses a little over 50 watt-hours, a small slice of a 1,000 watt-hour battery. The microwave is a heavy load but a short one. The problem is almost never capacity; it is whether the outlet can deliver the peak draw at all.

The table makes the shape of this market plain. Three of the five are 700-watt, 0.7 cubic foot machines, and the honest truth is that they cook almost identically. The differences between them are in the control panel layout, the finish, the door and the brand's parts support, which is why we rank them on fit and usability rather than pretending one 700-watt magnetron is meaningfully better than another.

The Toshiba stands apart because it gives you 900 cooking watts in a body that is still compact, which closes most of the gap with full-size microwaves on cook times. The cost of that is an input draw in the 1,400-watt range, which pushes it out of reach of the smaller power stations and some 2,000-watt inverter generators on their running rating. If you will only ever plug in at home, that does not matter. If you camp or prep for outages, it might.

The Panasonic is the outlier on purpose. At 1.2 cubic feet it is not a small microwave, but it is the most widely sold inverter microwave in the US, and it is the right comparison point for anyone wondering whether inverter technology is worth the extra size and price. For dorms and RVs it is usually too big. For a small kitchen with a real counter, it can be the better buy.

Use the input watt column you build yourself, from the label, as the deciding column when the microwave is going anywhere near a battery. Cooking watts tell you how fast dinner heats; input watts tell you whether it heats at all.

sections.h: Inverter Microwaves: What They Fix and What They Do Not

blocks.p: An inverter microwave replaces the heavy transformer with an electronic power supply that can run the magnetron at partial output continuously. Panasonic has built its microwave line around this design for years. At 50 percent power, an inverter model actually delivers roughly half power the whole time, instead of blasting at full power for a few seconds and then shutting off. The practical result is more even reheating and defrosting: the edges of a frozen block do not cook while the middle stays icy, and leftovers reheat without the rubbery rim.

For off-grid use, the inverter design has a second benefit that gets less attention. Because the magnetron can run at reduced output, a lower power setting genuinely lowers the draw from the outlet rather than just averaging it out. On a power station that cannot handle full input, dropping an inverter microwave to a medium setting can bring the load within limits. A conventional microwave cannot do that, because every on-cycle hits full draw. Owners running inverter microwaves on battery systems commonly report this as the deciding advantage.

Do not confuse the microwave's inverter with the power inverter in your RV or truck. They are unrelated. The power inverter converts 12-volt battery power to 120-volt household power, and for any microwave it should be a pure sine wave unit. Modified sine wave inverters can make microwaves run hot, buzz, cook unevenly, or fail outright, and inverter microwaves with sensitive electronics are the least tolerant of a dirty waveform. Our guide to the [best power inverter](/best-power-inverter/) covers sizing a pure sine unit for this kind of load.

What an inverter microwave does not fix is peak input at full power. The Panasonic NN-SN65KB at its 1,200-watt rating still draws in the 1,500-watt range at high power, more than any compact model on this list. And inverter microwaves in the compact size class are scarce in the US; most inverter models start around 1.2 cubic feet. If you need genuinely small and genuinely inverter, the choice narrows quickly, and you may have to accept one or the other.

Our view: if you mostly reheat coffee and leftovers at home, the inverter premium is not worth paying for a small microwave. If you defrost a lot, cook delicate food, or plan to run the microwave on a battery system where controlling peak draw matters, the inverter design earns its keep, and it is worth making counter space for it.

sections.h: Running a Small Microwave on a 1,000 to 1,800 Watt Power Station

blocks.p: Portable power stations are where most people discover the cooking-watts trap. A station with a 1,000-watt continuous output looks like it should run a 700-watt microwave easily, but with an input draw around 1,000 to 1,100 watts and a start-up surge on top, it is right at the edge or over it. Some stations ride through, especially those with a generous surge rating, and some shut down every time the magnetron starts. A 1,000-watt station is the wrong buy if a microwave is on your list.

The comfortable range starts around 1,500 watts continuous for a 700-watt microwave and 1,800 watts or more for a 900-watt model. At that output, the station has headroom for the surge and is not running its inverter at the limit, which keeps the fan quieter and the electronics cooler. Most current 1,800-watt-class stations from the major brands have surge ratings well above their continuous figure, which is what you want. Our pillar guide to the [best portable power station](/best-portable-power-station/) lists continuous and surge output for each pick, and that is the comparison to make.

Some stations offer a power-lifting or surge-boost mode that lets resistive loads like kettles run above the rated output by lowering voltage. That mode is designed for heating elements, not microwaves. A microwave's transformer and electronics need proper voltage, and running one on a voltage-lowered output can mean weak cooking or a fault. Leave those modes off for microwaves unless the station's manufacturer explicitly says otherwise.

Capacity is the easier half. A microwave is a brief load, so a 1,000 to 2,000 watt-hour battery handles a surprising amount of reheating. Ten three-minute sessions on a 700-watt model use roughly 500 watt-hours, give or take efficiency losses. If you plan to use the station for outages as well, our guide to [power stations for home backup](/best-portable-power-station-for-home-backup/) covers how to size for a fridge, lights and a microwave together.

Plug the microwave directly into an AC outlet on the station, not through a power strip or a thin extension cord. Do not run it at the same time as another large load like a space heater or a coffee maker; total draw is what trips the station. And if the station has a separate 20-amp outlet or a higher-rated port, use that one for the microwave.

sections.h: Running a Small Microwave on a Generator

blocks.p: A 2,000-watt inverter generator is the classic camping and tailgating size, and it is a good match for a 700-watt microwave. These generators typically carry a running rating around 1,600 to 1,800 watts with the 2,000-watt figure being the peak, so a microwave drawing about 1,100 watts leaves room for a phone charger and a few lights. A 900-watt microwave at around 1,400 watts input is workable but tight; add a coffee maker or a small electric heater and the generator will overload. The picks in our [best generator for camping](/best-generator-for-camping/) guide are sized with this in mind.

Use an inverter generator rather than an open-frame contractor unit when possible. Inverter generators produce cleaner power with steadier voltage and frequency, which microwaves and their electronic controls tolerate better. Many also have an economy mode that idles the engine down at light load. Economy mode can cause a hesitation when the microwave starts, and some owners turn it off for the minutes the microwave is running so the engine is already at speed when the load hits.
SAFETY FIRST
Generators run outside, always.

Never run a generator in a garage, under an awning, in a tent vestibule or inside an RV or truck bed cap, even with doors open. Carbon monoxide kills quickly and without warning. Keep the generator well away from windows, doors and vents, with the exhaust pointed away from where people are, and keep working carbon monoxide alarms in the RV or home.

In an RV with a built-in generator, the microwave is often already on the generator circuit, and the limit is usually the generator's running rating and what else is on at the time. The rooftop air conditioner is the usual culprit when a microwave trips the breaker. Running the AC and the microwave together on a smaller onboard generator is often more than it can handle, and many RVers simply pause the AC for the few minutes the microwave runs. Our [best RV generator](/best-rv-generator/) guide explains which sizes can carry both loads.

If you plan to power a home microwave from a generator during an outage, use heavy-duty outdoor extension cords run from the generator to the appliance, or a transfer switch or interlock installed by a licensed electrician and permitted where your local code requires it. Never backfeed a house through a dryer outlet or any other receptacle. It is illegal in most places, and it can energize the utility lines and kill a line worker.

sections.h: Fitting a Small Microwave in an RV, Van or Dorm

blocks.p: Countertop microwaves need air. The cooling fan pulls air in and pushes it out through vents on the sides, top or back, and the manual for each model specifies minimum clearances around the cabinet. Those numbers vary by model, commonly a few inches on the top and sides and at least an inch or so behind, and they are not suggestions. A microwave tucked into a tight cabinet with no airflow overheats, trips its thermal cutoff, and has a shorter life. Read the clearance table in your specific model's manual before you build around it.

RV factory microwaves are often over-the-range or built-in units with trim kits designed for the cabinet opening. Replacing one with a countertop model sounds easy and often is not, because the opening is sized for a different body and may not provide the airflow a countertop unit expects. If you are replacing a built-in RV microwave, start with the RV manufacturer's or the original microwave maker's replacement and trim kit, or have an RV technician confirm a countertop model will fit with its stated clearances.

A countertop microwave in a moving vehicle needs to be secured. A 25-pound box on a counter becomes a projectile in a hard stop, and the glass turntable tray should come out and be packed for travel. Owners use strap kits, L-brackets screwed into the counter or a shelf with a lip, but whatever you choose should not block the vents. The microwave also needs its own 120-volt outlet sized for the load; in an RV, that means a dedicated circuit or one you know is not shared with the air conditioner, and on shore power, adequate amperage at the pedestal. Our RV power adapter guide covers what happens when you plug a 30-amp rig into a 15-amp outlet.

In a van or truck running off a battery bank and inverter, a 700-watt microwave pulling around 1,050 watts at 120 volts asks roughly 90 to 100 amps or more from a 12-volt battery once inverter losses are included. That requires properly sized cable, fusing and a battery able to deliver that current. A lithium bank handles it far better than lead-acid; see our lithium RV battery guide. This is not a cigarette-lighter project, and if you are not comfortable with DC wiring and fuse sizing, have an RV or marine electrician install it.

Dorms are simpler but have their own rules. Many colleges restrict microwave wattage or capacity, or ban personal microwaves in favor of a shared one or a microwave-fridge combo unit. Check the housing policy before you buy. Plug the microwave directly into a wall outlet, not into a power strip with a fridge, laptop and space heater on it, and do not share a circuit with another heating appliance if the breaker keeps tripping.

sections.h: Which Small Microwave Should You Buy?

blocks.p: **For most small kitchens and apartments,** buy the Toshiba EM925A5A. It gives you 900 cooking watts in a compact body, which means cook times close to a full-size microwave, and its control panel is straightforward. The only reason to pass is if it will run on a power station under 1,800 watts or a 2,000-watt generator with other loads; then step down to 700 watts.

**For a dorm, an office or anything powered by a battery,** buy the BLACK+DECKER EM720CB7. Its 700-watt rating keeps input draw around the 1,000-watt range, the footprint is one of the smallest in its class, and it has simple controls that anyone can use. It is the most sensible microwave to pair with a 1,500-watt-class power station or a 2,000-watt inverter generator. If you prefer a stainless finish to match appliances, the GE JES1072SHSS is the same idea with a different look.

**For occasional use on the lowest budget,** the Commercial Chef 0.7 cubic foot model does the job: it heats food, it is light enough to move around, and its controls are clear. It is the right buy for a garage, a workshop or a cabin where it gets used a few times a month, not the right buy as the only microwave in a busy household.

**For the best reheating results and a counter with room to spare,** the Panasonic NN-SN65KB is the upgrade. Its inverter design genuinely improves defrosting and reheating, and on a battery system a lower power setting genuinely lowers the draw. It is not small and it needs a big power source at full power, so it fits kitchens and large RVs rather than dorms and vans.

Whichever you choose, read the input watt figure on the rating label before it goes anywhere near a power station, inverter or generator, and size the power source to that number with headroom. That one habit prevents nearly every off-grid microwave problem we hear about.

mistakes: Sizing the power source to cooking watts

The number on the front of the microwave is cooking power. Input draw is roughly 1.5 times higher, so a 700-watt model pulls about 1,000 to 1,100 watts and a 1,000-watt model around 1,500. Read the rating label and size the power station, inverter or generator to that input figure, plus headroom for start-up surge.
Running it on a modified sine wave inverter

Microwaves, and inverter microwaves in particular, expect a clean sine wave. On a cheap modified sine wave inverter they can buzz, run hot, cook poorly or fail. In a truck, van or RV running off a battery bank, the inverter feeding it should be a pure sine wave unit sized well above the microwave's input draw.
Boxing it into a cabinet with no airflow

Every countertop microwave needs the clearances listed in its manual on the top, sides and back so the cooling fan can move air. Tucking one into a tight RV cabinet or a bookshelf without that space leads to overheating, nuisance shutdowns and a shorter life. Measure the space and subtract the clearances before choosing a model.
Running a generator too close to the RV or house

A generator powering a microwave belongs outdoors, well away from windows, doors and vents, with the exhaust pointed away from people. Never run it in a garage, under an awning or inside a truck cap. Carbon monoxide builds up fast and without warning, so keep working carbon monoxide alarms wherever people are sleeping.
Stacking the microwave with other big loads

A power station or small generator that runs the microwave alone may trip when the coffee maker, space heater or RV air conditioner is running too. Total draw is what counts. Run the microwave by itself for its few minutes, then switch the other loads back on, and plug it directly into the source rather than a crowded power strip.
bottomLine: For a small kitchen on household power, the Toshiba EM925A5A gives you near full-size speed in a compact body. For anything that runs on a battery or a camping generator, the 700-watt BLACK+DECKER EM720CB7 or GE JES1072SHSS is the easier machine to power, and the Panasonic NN-SN65KB is the upgrade if even reheating matters and you have room. Whatever you buy, read the input watts on the label, size the power source to that number with headroom, keep generators outside, and give the microwave the airflow its manual asks for.

faqs.q: What size microwave counts as small?
faqs.a: Compact microwaves generally run from about 0.6 to 0.9 cubic feet. A 0.7 cubic foot model is the classic dorm and office size and usually has 700 cooking watts, while a 0.9 cubic foot model is a bit larger and usually rated around 900 watts. Exterior dimensions vary by brand, so measure your space and check the clearances in the manual before buying.

faqs.q: How many watts does a 1000W microwave actually use?
faqs.a: A microwave rated at 1,000 cooking watts typically draws around 1,500 watts from the outlet, because the transformer and magnetron lose a lot of energy as heat. The exact figure is on the rating label inside the door or on the back. Size any power station, inverter or generator to that input number, with at least 20 percent headroom.

faqs.q: Can a 1,000 watt power station run a small microwave?
faqs.a: Usually not reliably. A 700-watt microwave draws around 1,000 to 1,100 watts plus a start-up surge, which puts it at or above the limit of a 1,000-watt station. Some stations ride through and many shut down. A station rated around 1,500 watts continuous is the comfortable minimum for a 700-watt model, and 1,800 watts or more for a 900-watt model.

faqs.q: Can I run a microwave on a 2,000 watt inverter generator?
faqs.a: Yes, a 700-watt microwave runs comfortably on a typical 2,000-watt inverter generator, whose running rating is usually around 1,600 to 1,800 watts. A 900-watt model is workable but leaves little room for other loads. Keep the generator outdoors, far from windows and doors, and turn off economy mode if the microwave hesitates when starting.

faqs.q: Is there a portable microwave for a car?
faqs.a: Most products marketed as car microwaves are heated lunch boxes that warm food slowly through a heating plate. True 12-volt microwaves have existed but are rare, and we could not find one in wide distribution to recommend. A real microwave in a vehicle needs a 120-volt model, a pure sine wave inverter, heavy cabling and a battery bank able to supply around 100 amps at 12 volts.

For even reheating and defrosting, yes. An inverter microwave runs at genuinely reduced power on lower settings, so food heats more evenly. On a battery system, lower settings also genuinely reduce draw. The catch is size and price: most inverter models start around 1.2 cubic feet, so they are hard to fit in dorms and vans. For basic reheating, a conventional compact is fine.

faqs.q: What do I need to know about microwaves in an RV?
faqs.a: Check whether your RV microwave is a built-in or over-the-range unit with a trim kit, because swapping in a countertop model often needs a different opening and airflow. Secure any countertop model for travel and remove the glass tray. Make sure the outlet and circuit can carry the input draw, and avoid running it with the air conditioner on a small generator.
